chapters.title: Numbers up to 20
chapters.tagline: Build a ten, count the loose ones and find neighbours.
outcomes: I can show numbers up to 20.
I can find before, after and between.
I can compare numbers and skip-count.

vocab.meaning: A full ten frame. 10 counters.
Before is one less. After is one more.
In the middle of two numbers.
Count in jumps, like 2, 4, 6, 8.

see.title: A full ten
text: A full frame is one ten.

see.title: Ten and some more
text: Put the rest in the next frame.

try.prompt: Show 13. Fill a ten, then add 3 more.
try.success: Yes! 10 and 3 more is 13.
try.hint: Fill the first frame to 10. Then add 3 more in the next frame.

try.prompt: Which number comes after 16? Tap it.
try.success: Yes! After 16 comes 17.
try.hint: Find 16. The number after is one step to the right.

try.prompt: Which number is between 11 and 13? Tap it.
try.success: Yes! 12 is between 11 and 13.
try.hint: Say the numbers in order: 11, then ?, then 13.

parents.idea: Your child builds numbers to 20 as a ten and some ones, and learns what comes before, after and between. Skip counting by 2s is the start of times tables.
parents.slip: Counting teen numbers as one big group and losing count. Fill a ten first, then count only the extra ones.

tryAtHome.title: Egg-box teens
steps: Use an egg box or two rows of 5 for a ten frame.
Ask your child to fill a ten with buttons.
Add 4 more on the next row. Say, "10 and 4 is 14".
Ask which number comes before 14 and which comes after.

chapters.title: Add and take away
chapters.tagline: Join groups, remove objects and find a hidden part.
outcomes: I can add two small groups.
I can find what is left.
I can find a missing part.

vocab.meaning: Put groups together to find how many in all.
Remove some. Count what is left.
The part you cannot see yet.

see.title: Take away
text: There were 7. Blue ones are taken away.

see.title: Hop to add
text: You land on 5. So 3 and 2 make 5.

try.prompt: Join 4 and 3. Show how many in all.
try.success: Yes! 4 and 3 make 7.
try.hint: Count 4, then keep counting 3 more: 5, 6, 7.

try.prompt: Make 8 with two parts. Use the plus buttons.
try.success: Yes! The two parts make 8.
try.hint: Try 5 in one part and 3 in the other.

try.prompt: The right side has 9. Add to the left side to make it level.
try.success: Yes! 4 and 5 make 9. The missing part is 5.
try.hint: Add one at a time. Stop when both sides match.

parents.idea: Your child joins two groups, takes some away, and finds a missing part. They use objects first. Numbers up to 10 are enough.
parents.slip: Counting all again instead of counting on. Say the bigger number, then count on: 4 ... 5, 6, 7.

tryAtHome.title: Snack sums
steps: Put 4 crackers on a plate and 3 on another.
Join them. Ask, "How many altogether?"
Eat 2. Ask how many are left.
Hide some under a cup. Ask how many are hidden.

chapters.title: Flat shapes and solid things
chapters.tagline: Connect shapes to real objects and simple position clues.
outcomes: I can count sides and corners.
I can recognise a solid by how it moves.
I can join shapes to make a picture.

vocab.meaning: A straight edge of a flat shape.
A pointy place where two sides meet.
A shape you can hold, like a ball or a box.
To turn over and over, like a ball.

see.title: Count sides and corners
text: A triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners.
A square and a rectangle have 4.
A circle has no sides and no corners.

see.title: Solid things
text: Solids are shapes you can hold.
A ball is a sphere. A box is a cube or a cuboid.

see.title: Rolls or slides?
text: A cube has flat faces. It slides, it does not roll.

see.title: Shapes make a picture
text: A square, a triangle, a rectangle and a circle.
Put them together and they make a house.

try.prompt: Sort the shapes by corners.
try.success: Yes! Triangle 3, square and rectangle 4, circle and oval none.
try.hint: Touch each corner with a finger and count.

try.prompt: Which solids can roll? Which cannot?
try.success: Yes! A sphere and a cylinder roll. A cube and a cuboid do not.
try.hint: Think of a ball and a tin of beans. Do they roll?

parents.idea: Your child counts the sides and corners of flat shapes, names solids by how they move, and builds pictures from shapes.
parents.slip: Mixing up a flat shape with a solid, like circle and sphere. A circle is flat. A sphere is a ball you can hold.

tryAtHome.title: Roll or slide
steps: Find a ball, a tin, a box and a dice.
Ask your child to guess which will roll.
Push each one gently across the floor.
Name each solid together.

chapters.title: Long, heavy and full
chapters.tagline: Compare objects with common units and informal balances.
outcomes: I can compare lengths and sizes.
I can measure with equal blocks.
I can compare weight and capacity.

vocab.meaning: Long goes further. Short is not so far.
Heavy is hard to lift. Light is easy.
Full holds all it can. Empty holds nothing.

see.title: Longer and shorter
text: Line the pencils up at one end.

see.title: Measure with equal blocks
text: Use blocks that are all the same size.
Count them. This row is 5 blocks long.

see.title: Heavy and light
text: The heavy side of a balance goes down.

see.title: Full and empty
text: Full means it is up to the top.
Empty means there is no water.

try.prompt: Sort: which are long or tall? Which are short?
try.success: Yes! You compared lengths and heights.
try.hint: Which one reaches further, or goes higher?

try.prompt: A rope is 6 blocks long. Hop 6 blocks from 0. Tap where it ends.
try.success: Yes! 6 equal blocks long.
try.hint: Start at 0. Count one hop for each block.

try.prompt: Make the balance level. The right side is heavier.
try.success: Yes! Now both sides are the same weight.
try.hint: Add one at a time to the left until it is level.

try.prompt: Which is heavy? Which is light?
try.success: Yes! A rock is heavy. A balloon is light.
try.hint: Which would be harder to lift?

parents.idea: Your child compares length, weight and how full things are. Then they measure with equal blocks, a first step to rulers and scales.
parents.slip: Measuring with unequal things, like different-sized blocks, or not starting at the same end. Use the same block and line up the start.

tryAtHome.title: Measure the teddy
steps: Use 10 equal blocks or spoons.
Lay them end to end beside a teddy.
Count how many blocks long the teddy is.
Measure a shoe. Which is longer?

chapters.title: Find the pattern
chapters.tagline: Repeat a group, fill a gap and predict a growing picture.
outcomes: I can continue a repeating group.
I can fill a gap in a pattern.
I can spot a broken rule.

vocab.meaning: A group of pictures that repeats.
A missing spot in a pattern.
What the pattern does each time.

see.title: Repeat the group
text: The same group again and again.

see.title: A broken rule
text: Then a ball. That breaks the rule.

try.prompt: Star, star, heart. Pick what comes next.
try.success: Yes! Star, star, heart. Again!
try.hint: The group is star, star, heart. Which one finishes it?

try.prompt: Fill both gaps in the pattern.
try.success: Yes! Ball, apple, ball, apple, ball, apple.
try.hint: Say it from the start. The pattern is ball, apple.

try.prompt: The pattern is broken. Put the right picture in the gap.
try.success: Yes! Fish, ball, fish, ball. The gap is a fish.
try.hint: A fish goes before every ball.

parents.idea: Your child continues a repeating pattern, fills a gap, and spots a picture that breaks the rule. Growing patterns lead to number rules later.
parents.slip: Guessing a gap without saying the whole group. Say the pattern from the start every time.

tryAtHome.title: Clap and stamp
steps: Clap, clap, stamp. Clap, clap, stamp.
Ask your child to carry on.
Make a mistake on purpose. Ask, "What went wrong?"
Draw a colour pattern and cover one part.

chapters.title: Follow the picture clues
chapters.tagline: Use positions, arrows and two visible clues.
outcomes: I can find a place in a row.
I can choose a picture using two clues.
I can follow arrows on a map.

vocab.meaning: A small hint that helps you find the answer.
First is at the start. Last is at the end.
It points which way to go.

see.title: Places in a row
text: The ball is 1st. The apple is 2nd.
The star is 3rd. The heart is 4th.

see.title: Use two clues
text: Only the apple is red and round.

see.title: Follow the arrows
text: Arrows tell the robot where to go.
North is up. East is right.
Go up, up, then right, right to reach the goal.

try.prompt: Put the picture that is red and round in the first box.
try.success: Yes! Only the apple is red and round.
try.hint: Check clue 1 (red). Then check clue 2 (round).

try.prompt: Make the robot reach the goal. Add arrows, then press Run.
try.success: Yes! The robot reached the goal.
try.hint: There is a wall in the middle. Go up, up, then right, right.

try.prompt: The row is ball, apple, star, heart, fish. Tap the place of the fish.
try.success: Yes! The fish is 5th. It is last.
try.hint: Count from the left: 1, 2, 3, 4, and then the fish.

parents.idea: Your child finds a place in a row, picks a picture using two clues, and follows arrows. These are the first steps of logic and coding.
parents.slip: Using only one clue. Say each clue aloud and cross out pictures that do not match.

tryAtHome.title: Treasure hunt
steps: Hide a toy in the room.
Give two clues: "It is soft. It is on the sofa."
Then give arrow steps: two steps forward, one step left.
Swap and let your child give the clues.

chapters.title: Days, months and clocks
chapters.tagline: Talk about daily routines, weekday order and whole hours together.
outcomes: I can say the day before or after.
I can put familiar months in order.
I can recognise a whole hour on a clock.

vocab.meaning: 7 days. Monday to Sunday, then it starts again.
There are 12 months in a year.
The long hand points up to 12. The short hand shows the hour.

see.title: Day and night
text: The sun is out in the day.
The moon is out at night.
Each day has a day time and a night time.

see.title: Seven days make a week
text: After Sunday a new week starts.

see.title: Twelve months make a year
text: There are 12 months in a year.
January is first. December is last.

try.prompt: Today is Tuesday. Tap tomorrow.
try.success: Yes! After Tuesday comes Wednesday.
try.hint: The days go in order: Monday, Tuesday, then the next one.

try.prompt: Show 4 o'clock. Move the hands or use the buttons.
try.success: 4 o'clock: the long hand is on 12 and the short hand is on 4.
try.hint: Keep the long hand on 12. Move the short hand to 4.

try.prompt: Which month comes after March? Tap its number.
try.success: Yes! April is the 4th month, after March.
try.hint: January 1, February 2, March 3. What is next?

parents.idea: Your child talks about day and night, puts days and months in order, and reads a whole hour on a clock. Practise and Check use the Class 1 time questions at level 1, so sit alongside your child.
parents.slip: Mixing up the order of months or days. Sing the days in order. Use a wall calendar and tick off each day.

tryAtHome.title: Daily routine clock
steps: At breakfast, say "It is 7 o'clock" and show the clock.
Ask, "What day is it? What day comes next?"
Point to today on a wall calendar.
Match one routine to an hour, like bedtime at 8 o'clock.
